title: Who wears them
hookLine: traditionally men from bar mitzvah; in many non-Orthodox communities women wear them too

cards: Two synagogues on the same street, the same weekday morning.
In the first, the men's section is full of arms wrapped in black straps, fathers next to sons, a boy of twelve putting them on for the first time while his grandfather watches.
The women pray on their own side, without tefillin. In the second, a woman in her forties winds a strap around her arm, next to a teenage girl doing the same. Both rooms pray the same prayers.
Each follows a reading it has thought through. And both are Jewish.

teach.b: Traditional Jewish law says men are obligated to wear tefillin from bar mitzvah, which the Mishnah puts at thirteen, the age of commandments. In some communities, boys start practicing a little before.
Women, in traditional law, are exempt.
Not forbidden: exempt, under a general rule that women are exempt from positive commandments tied to a set time, and tefillin are worn by day.
Then comes a surprising line in the Talmud: Michal, the daughter of King Saul, wore tefillin, and the sages did not protest. Rabbis argued for centuries over what to make of that.
Some said a woman may choose to take on the practice; later codes, like the Rema's notes to the Shulchan Aruch, discouraged it.
Today each community answers with its own reasons. Orthodox communities generally keep the traditional practice: men wear tefillin, women don't.
Conservative Judaism teaches that women may take on the commandment, and its law committee has ruled they can be equally obligated, so in many Conservative synagogues, women wear tefillin.
In Reform and other liberal communities, tefillin are a personal choice for anyone; some people of all genders wear them, and many don't wear them at all.

Some Jews wear them only now and then, and outreach volunteers on city streets offer to help a passing Jewish man put them on for a minute. All of these communities care about the same verse and the same boxes.
They differ over who is bound by it. Learning that a custom isn't yours is not the same as thinking it's wrong.

how: In Orthodox communities, men and boys from bar mitzvah wear tefillin each weekday morning. In many Conservative and liberal communities, women may wear them too, and in Reform communities wearing them is a personal choice.

a small skullcap worn to show respect before God

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.

s: traditional Jewish law forbids women to wear tefillin
it treats women as exempt, and later codes discouraged it; that's different from a biblical ban.
the Talmud mentions a woman who wore tefillin
Michal, the daughter of King Saul, and the sages did not protest.
all Jewish communities practice tefillin the same way
Orthodox, Conservative and Reform communities answer who wears them differently.

games.q: you're visiting a friend's synagogue, and they do tefillin differently from what you grew up with. what do you do?
o: tell them they're doing it wrong.
ask what the custom means to them.
games.why: there's no single right answer in the text. but every community here cares about the same verse; asking is how respect starts.

practice: Think of a practice you've seen done differently from how you'd do it: a holiday, a meal, a way of praying, a way of mourning. Before you judge it, picture the people who love it, and ask what it means to them.

wordCard.voice: Tefillin, the black straps and boxes traditionally worn by Jewish men from bar mitzvah, and today by women too in many non-Orthodox communities.

orig.note: Hebrew: custom, a practice handed down in a community.

carryVoice: Your line: customs differ, respect holds. Asking comes before deciding. Day one hundred forty-three, done.
